assumptions.assumption: A 2015-built, sprinklered warehouse with 400A/240V 3-phase power makes lithium charging/swap compliance an incremental cost (tens of thousands, a few weeks), so a 100-300 pack swap room can open at 768 Ceres within the pilot's first quarter.
assumptions.why_it_may_be_wrong: The 2025 California Fire Code (in force since Jan 2026) treats this as a regulated use, not a tenant fit-out. CFC 320 requires an operational permit above 15 cubic feet of loose lithium batteries — a Lightning MK.II pack is 74V/45Ah (~3.3 kWh, ~40 lb, roughly 0.6-0.9 cu ft), so the threshold is crossed at ~20 packs, and a SF-scale swap room (300+ subscribers) holds 165-1,000 kWh. Above the limited-container thresholds CFC 320 requires a fire-protection-engineer technical opinion & report evaluating thermal-runaway deflagration and the sprinkler design basis; the building's 'calculated sprinklers' were designed for the 2015 tenant's commodity class, not lithium storage, which FM/NFPA data treat as high-hazard (reduced pile height, in-rack or ESFR). CFC 322 (powered micromobility) only permits charging of LISTED devices using LISTED charging equipment, requires 18 inches between each removable pack unless isolated by fire-resistive material, one dedicated receptacle per charger (no power strips: 100 packs on 840W chargers = ~100 dedicated 15/20A circuits and ~84 kW), and a fire alarm using air-aspirating or radiant-energy detection. HMP's product pages claim DOT approval but no UL 2271/2849 for packs or UL 1310 for the 840W portable chargers; LAFD can simply refuse to permit charging of unlisted equipment.
assumptions.magnitude: One-time $40k-150k (FPE report $8-20k; aspirating detection + monitored alarm $20-50k; dedicated circuits $30-80k; sprinkler upgrade if required $50-150k) plus 3-9 months of LAFD/LADBS permitting during which the swap product cannot legally operate at scale. If packs/chargers are not listed, the charging use may be denied outright, leaving a $10k+/mo box that can only do repair and vehicle storage.
assumptions.cheap_test: Before LOI: (1) one email to the OEM requesting UL 2271/2849 certificates for every pack SKU and UL 1310/62368 for every charger SKU; (2) a pre-application call/meeting with LAFD Fire Prevention (Fire Development Services) describing 200 packs and 100 simultaneous chargers at 768 Ceres; (3) ask Lee & Associates for the sprinkler hydraulic placard (design density/area) and last 5-year certification; (4) a $2-3k feasibility letter from a fire protection engineer.
assumptions.hmp_internal_data_needed: Complete battery/charger SKU list with any listing certificates; peak count of loose packs on-site at 261 6th St and what SFFD actually permitted there (permit number, conditions, inspection findings); any thermal events or near-misses in SF; measured pack dimensions to compute cubic feet.

assumptions.assumption: Koreatown, Westlake and USC-area couriers — the majority of the named target riders — will detour to 8th & Ceres for battery swaps and service the way SoMa/FiDi riders walk into 261 6th St.
assumptions.why_it_may_be_wrong: SF geography does not transfer. 261 6th St sits within ~1.5 miles of nearly every SF delivery hotspot; 768 Ceres is ~4.3-5 miles from Wilshire/Vermont-Western, ~3.3 miles from MacArthur Park, ~3 miles from USC, across the 110 and through the DTLA one-way grid — 18-25 minutes each way on a 28 mph moped at dinner peak. A 40-50 minute round trip costs an LA courier 1.5-2.5 orders (~$12-20 gross) plus the swap fee, every swap. Riders who swap daily will not accept that; the realistic daily-swap catchment is DTLA core, Arts District, Fashion District and Little Tokyo (all within ~1.5 mi) — exactly the sub-area where Skid Row adjacency suppresses evening visits. K-town/Westlake/USC riders become occasional repair customers, not subscribers.
assumptions.magnitude: Effective swap catchment 40-60% smaller than the founder's target list implies; subscriber ramp plausibly half of any plan extrapolated from SF conversion rates; the Month 6/12 subscriber triggers would be set against the wrong denominator.
assumptions.cheap_test: Ride Wilshire/Western to 768 Ceres and back at 7pm and 9:30pm on a weekday with a timer; overlay DoorDash/Uber Eats hotspot maps on a 1.5/3/5-mile ring from the site; intercept-survey 30 couriers at K-town restaurant clusters (6th/Western, Wilshire/Vermont) asking the maximum detour minutes they would accept for a swap at a stated price; count e-mopeds parked outside DTLA vs K-town restaurants at 7pm.
assumptions.hmp_internal_data_needed: For SF subscribers: home/hotspot location vs distance to 261 6th St; swap frequency by distance band; churn by distance band; share of subscribers living or working more than 2 miles from the shop; whether anyone in SF regularly rides more than 15 minutes to swap.

assumptions.assumption: The depot can run rider-facing hours until ~10-11pm seven days a week, because that is when couriers finish dinner shifts and need swaps, repairs and replacement vehicles.
assumptions.why_it_may_be_wrong: The site's peak-demand window coincides with the block's peak-risk window. 8th & Ceres is one to two blocks south of the official Skid Row boundary (7th St); LAPD and aggregated data show Skid Row incidents peak late evening to early morning. The adjacent produce-district businesses operate roughly 1am-noon, so from 6pm to midnight the street is dark, empty and un-surveilled by neighbors. Staff closing at 10:30pm with $100-300k of fungible packs inside, and riders arriving with $3-5k vehicles and a phone, are both exposed. Two outcomes: riders refuse evening visits (demand shifts to midday when it is worth less to them), and evening staff are hard to hire and keep — expect a two-person minimum, a wage premium, and turnover. If hours contract to daytime, the 'replacement vehicle tonight' promise — the core of the Rider Center pitch — fails.
assumptions.magnitude: If SF's after-7pm share of swaps/service visits is 30-50% (needs data), that volume is at risk or displaced; evening labor +$3-5k/mo for two-person staffing; one assault or robbery of a rider outside the gate ends word-of-mouth in a tight courier community.
assumptions.cheap_test: Three evening site visits (Thu/Fri/Sat, 8-11pm) logging encampments, lighting, foot traffic and incidents within 300 ft of the door; request calls-for-service for the reporting district from the LAPD Central Division Senior Lead Officer; ask the 772 Ceres tenant and two produce neighbors about after-dark break-ins and whether they will operate after 6pm; check that streetlights on the 700-800 blocks of Ceres are working.
assumptions.hmp_internal_data_needed: Hourly distribution of swaps, service check-ins and replacement-vehicle handoffs at 261 6th St; share of revenue after 7pm; evening staff incident log; evening-shift attrition over 12 months; whether SoMa evening operations required any security measures beyond locks.

assumptions.assumption: A gate, cameras, alarm, indoor storage and vehicle GPS (~$15-30k one-time plus a monitored alarm) neutralize the theft risk of holding 100-300 packs and a replacement fleet at this address.
assumptions.why_it_may_be_wrong: The inventory is unusually attractive: a 40-lb pack resells for $500-1,000 with no registry, carries out by hand, and is not GPS-tracked (GPS is on vehicles). A box-truck break-in between 1am and 6am blends into produce-district truck and forklift traffic; 50 packs leave in ten minutes ($50-100k). The lot is only 9,091 SF against an 8,443 SF building — roughly 650 SF outdoors, so the 'electrical yard gate' is a driveway, not a secured queue: riders' own vehicles wait at the curb on Ceres while they are inside, and curb theft of a courier's moped is a business-ending review. Insurers writing lithium-inventory cover at this address will likely require monitored guard service or 24/7 staffing as protective conditions, which converts a one-time capex line into a recurring cost comparable to rent.
assumptions.magnitude: Recurring security $3-10k/mo (evening/overnight guard $25-35/hr, or 24/7 staffing), i.e. 30-100% of the $10k rent; single-event loss $50-100k of packs plus deductible; a rider-vehicle theft at the curb costs more in churn than in dollars.
assumptions.cheap_test: Three written quotes from LA guard/patrol companies for evening and overnight coverage at 768 Ceres; ask a commercial insurance broker for the minimum protective requirements to cover $200k of lithium inventory at this address; pull LAPD crime-mapping for commercial burglary and vehicle theft on the 700-900 blocks of Ceres/Crocker/Towne for the last 12 months; ask the neighbors what they spend on security.
assumptions.hmp_internal_data_needed: SF shrink log at 261 6th St: break-ins and attempts, packs lost, customer vehicles stolen from the curb, insurance claims filed, monthly security spend; how SoMa (also a high-incident area) actually performed, as the closest comparable.

assumptions.assumption: The landlord, the landlord's property insurer and HMP's own carrier will accept 'lithium battery charging/swap + electric motorcycle repair' as a permitted use at roughly standard terms, and the ~$10k/mo figure absorbs it.
assumptions.why_it_may_be_wrong: The building is marketed as showroom/industrial (the paired 768/772 listing is 'full service', ~43% office). Post-NYC-fire underwriting, many property carriers exclude or surcharge lithium charging operations, and landlords are inserting explicit 'no lithium battery charging/storage' clauses or requiring the tenant to carry the landlord's premium increase through NNN. A motorcycle repair use may also require an LADBS change of occupancy/CofO. HMP's own general liability and property policy may already exclude battery charging of unlisted equipment. None of this appears in a $10k/mo number, and asking rents on current listings are $16.80-19.20/SF/yr ($11.8k-13.5k/mo for 8,443 SF), so the base rent itself may be understated by 20-35%.
assumptions.magnitude: Insurance +$1-3k/mo and a possible NNN pass-through; rent gap $2-3.5k/mo vs listings; a landlord or carrier prohibition on lithium charging is a hard stop for the swap product; a CofO change adds 2-4 months.
assumptions.cheap_test: Before LOI, get in writing from Lee & Associates: the landlord's acceptance of lithium charging/swap and motorcycle repair as permitted use, the landlord's carrier's position, and lease type (NNN vs gross) with an itemized estimate; check ZIMAS for zoning and the current Certificate of Occupancy; obtain two quotes for HMP's property/GL at this address with declared kWh on-site.
assumptions.hmp_internal_data_needed: Current SF policy declarations and exclusions (carrier, premium, declared battery inventory, any lithium exclusions); the permitted-use language in the 261 6th St lease; any SFFD operational permit; loss history.

assumptions.assumption: 8,443 SF is open warehouse floor — 'far more than a pilot needs' — with a usable yard, so the pilot has room to grow into it.
assumptions.why_it_may_be_wrong: Listing data suggest otherwise in both directions. The building was completed in 2015 with '100% HVAC', a 'modern office layout' and two executive offices; the paired 768/772 listing reports 7,250 SF of office out of 16,887 SF, implying 768 may carry ~3,000-3,600 SF of built-out office. Open floor is then ~5,000 SF, of which a compliant battery room at 18-inch spacing consumes ~6 SF per pack (200 packs ≈ 1,200 SF plus aisles) before any fleet, repair bays or parts. The site is not oversized; it is mis-shaped — 35-45% of rent buys air-conditioned office that a depot does not need, and there is no yard for rider queueing or secured outdoor parking. Grade-level doors appear to be one per building, and Ceres Ave is a narrow produce-district street with early-morning truck congestion.
assumptions.magnitude: $3.5-4.5k/mo of the rent attributable to office space; usable floor 30-40% smaller than the headline; if the swap room and 100+ rental/replacement vehicles must fit, the site may actually be tight, which undercuts both the 'oversized' critique and the 'room to grow' story.
assumptions.cheap_test: Get the floor plan from the broker and walk the site with a tape measure: office SF, clear height, door count and width, yard SF, and whether a moped can be ridden in through the door; time a loading test at 7am when produce trucks are active.
assumptions.hmp_internal_data_needed: Square feet per stored vehicle, per repair bay and per charging pack at 261 6th St; vehicles and packs on-site at peak; repair throughput per bay, to size what the LA pilot actually needs.

assumptions.assumption: One consolidated hub at Ceres is the minimum viable footprint and is cheaper and simpler than a two-node model (small Koreatown swap point plus a low-cost warehouse in Vernon/Boyle Heights).
assumptions.why_it_may_be_wrong: A 800-1,500 SF Koreatown/Westlake storefront or light-industrial bay at ~$2.50-3.50/SF/mo ($2.5-5k/mo) plus a 3,000-4,000 SF Vernon/Boyle Heights warehouse at ~$1.10-1.40/SF/mo ($3.5-5.5k/mo) lands at $6-10k/mo — the same envelope as Ceres — but puts the swap point where the named riders actually are, isolates the fire-code-heavy charging room in cheap space with no rider traffic, and can be assembled from month-to-month or sublease deals instead of a 3-5 year commitment ($360-600k of lease liability on Ceres). The counterarguments (split staff, two fire permits, less co-location of repair and swap) are real but are exactly the kind of thing a 90-day pop-up can test before any lease.
assumptions.magnitude: Does not change total occupancy cost much but changes the risk shape: swap demand validated in the rider's neighborhood, lease exposure cut by 60-80%, and Skid Row exposure limited to staff and inventory rather than customers. Likely moves the decision from GO to CONDITIONAL GO rather than to NO-GO.
assumptions.cheap_test: Pull ten sub-1,500 SF Koreatown/Westlake listings and five Vernon/Boyle Heights warehouse listings this week; run a 60-90 day van-based swap pop-up in a K-town parking lot at dinner peak (no lease) and count paying swaps per night; compare against the DTLA-only catchment from a pop-up near 7th/Los Angeles St.
assumptions.hmp_internal_data_needed: SF revenue and margin split by service line (swap subscription vs repair vs rental); share of swap visits that also generate a repair ticket (the co-location value); how often a subscriber uses replacement vehicles; staffing per node in SF.
